claim: The entorhinal cortex, in particular neurons in layer V, allegedly mediate transfer of information from the hippocampus to the neocortex, underlying long-term memory.
source: The entorhinal cortex, in particular neurons in layer V, allegedly mediate transfer of information from the hippocampus to the neocortex, underlying long-term memory.
evidence: This is a statement about the proposed function of entorhinal cortex layer V neurons, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: The hippocampal-cortical circuit comprises a hippocampal output recipient layer Vb and a cortical projecting layer Va.
source: Recently, this circuit has been shown to comprise a hippocampal output recipient layer Vb and a cortical projecting layer Va.
evidence: This statement references recent research findings about the circuit organization.

claim: MEC, particularly its dorsal part, processes allocentric spatial information.
source: MEC, particularly its dorsal part, processes allocentric spatial information, whereas the corresponding part of LEC processes information representing elements of episodes.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional properties of MEC based on established knowledge.

claim: The corresponding part of LEC processes information representing elements of episodes.
source: MEC, particularly its dorsal part, processes allocentric spatial information, whereas the corresponding part of LEC processes information representing elements of episodes.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional properties of LEC based on established knowledge.

claim: Connections from layer Vb-to-Va neurons are stronger in dorsal LEC compared with dorsal MEC.
source: Using identical experimental approaches, we show that connections from layer Vb-to-Va neurons are stronger in dorsal LEC compared with dorsal MEC, suggesting different operating principles in these two regions.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding of the study, supported by electrophysiological and anatomical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Different operating principles exist in LEC and MEC based on the differences in Vb-to-Va connectivity.
source: Using identical experimental approaches, we show that connections from layer Vb-to-Va neurons are stronger in dorsal LEC compared with dorsal MEC, suggesting different operating principles in these two regions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed connectivity differences.

claim: The findings imply a potential difference in how LEC and MEC mediate episodic systems consolidation.
source: Although further in vivo experiments are needed, our findings imply a potential difference in how LEC and MEC mediate episodic systems consolidation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, explicitly noted as requiring further in vivo experiments.

claim: Memory consolidation involves gradual reorganization of interconnected brain regions.
source: This memory maturation process, called memory consolidation, involves gradual reorganization of interconnected brain regions: memories that are initially depending on hippocampus become increasingly dependent on cortical networks over time (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Frankland and Bontempi, 2005.

claim: Memories that are initially depending on hippocampus become increasingly dependent on cortical networks over time.
source: This memory maturation process, called memory consolidation, involves gradual reorganization of interconnected brain regions: memories that are initially depending on hippocampus become increasingly dependent on cortical networks over time (Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Frankland and Bontempi, 2005.

claim: The canonical hippocampal-cortical output circuit via the entorhinal cortex is crucial to mediate long-term memory storage and recall.
source: they all share a canonical hippocampal-cortical output circuit via the entorhinal cortex (EC), which is crucial to mediate long-term memory storage and recall (Buzsáki, 1996; Eichenbaum et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Buzsáki, 1996 and Eichenbaum et al., 2012.

claim: A non-fornical hippocampal-cortical output route is mediated by layer V of the EC in monkeys.
source: The existence of this circuit was originally proposed based on the ground-breaking report of a non-fornical hippocampal-cortical output route mediated by layer V (LV) of the EC in monkeys (Rosene and Van Hoesen, 1977), which was later confirmed also in rodents (Köhler, 1985; Kosel et al., 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rosene and Van Hoesen, 1977.

claim: The non-fornical hippocampal-cortical output route mediated by layer V of the EC was later confirmed in rodents.
source: The existence of this circuit was originally proposed based on the ground-breaking report of a non-fornical hippocampal-cortical output route mediated by layer V (LV) of the EC in monkeys (Rosene and Van Hoesen, 1977), which was later confirmed also in rodents (Köhler, 1985; Kosel et al., 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Köhler, 1985 and Kosel et al., 1982.

claim: MEC processes allocentric, mainly spatial information.
source: MEC processes allocentric, mainly spatial information, whereas LEC represents the time and content of episodes (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Hafting et al., 2005; Montchal et al., 2019; Tsao et al., 2018; Tsao et al., 2013; Xu and Wilson, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: LEC represents the time and content of episodes.
source: MEC processes allocentric, mainly spatial information, whereas LEC represents the time and content of episodes (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011; Hafting et al., 2005; Montchal et al., 2019; Tsao et al., 2018; Tsao et al., 2013; Xu and Wilson, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: LV in both MEC and LEC can be genetically and connectionally divided into two sublayers: layer Vb and layer Va.
source: Recently, we and others have shown that LV in both MEC and LEC can be genetically and connectionally divided into two sublayers: a deep layer Vb (LVb), which contains neurons receiving projections from the hippocampus, and a superficial layer Va (LVa), which originates the main projections out to forebrain cortical and subcortical structures (Ohara et al., 2018; Ramsden et al., 2015; Sürmeli et al., 2015; Wozny et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies including the authors' own work.

claim: Layer Vb contains neurons receiving projections from the hippocampus.
source: Recently, we and others have shown that LV in both MEC and LEC can be genetically and connectionally divided into two sublayers: a deep layer Vb (LVb), which contains neurons receiving projections from the hippocampus, and a superficial layer Va (LVa), which originates the main projections out to forebrain cortical and subcortical structures (Ohara et al., 2018; Ramsden et al., 2015; Sürmeli et al., 2015; Wozny et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Layer Va originates the main projections out to forebrain cortical and subcortical structures.
source: Recently, we and others have shown that LV in both MEC and LEC can be genetically and connectionally divided into two sublayers: a deep layer Vb (LVb), which contains neurons receiving projections from the hippocampus, and a superficial layer Va (LVa), which originates the main projections out to forebrain cortical and subcortical structures (Ohara et al., 2018; Ramsden et al., 2015; Sürmeli et al., 2015; Wozny et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: For the hippocampal-cortical dialogue to function, a projection from LVb to LVa neurons is necessary.
source: These results indicate that for the hippocampal-cortical dialogue to function we need to postulate a projection from LVb to LVa neurons.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the circuit organization described.

claim: The existence of a LVb-LVa circuit is supported by transsynaptic viral tracing in rats.
source: Although the existence of such a LVb-LVa circuit is supported by our previous study using transsynaptic viral tracing in rats (Ohara et al., 2018), experimental evidence for functional connectivity from LVb-to-Va in LEC and MEC is still lacking.
evidence: This statement references the authors' previous study using viral tracing.

claim: Experimental evidence for functional connectivity from LVb-to-Va in LEC and MEC was lacking prior to this study.
source: Although the existence of such a LVb-LVa circuit is supported by our previous study using transsynaptic viral tracing in rats (Ohara et al., 2018), experimental evidence for functional connectivity from LVb-to-Va in LEC and MEC is still lacking.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The connectivity from LVb to LVa is prominent in dorsal LEC but apparently sparse in dorsal parts of MEC.
source: To our surprise, we found differences in the postulated intrinsic LVb-LVa pathway between the two entorhinal subdivisions: the connectivity is prominent in dorsal LEC but is apparently sparse in dorsal parts of MEC.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Intrinsic circuits from LVb to layers II and III are very similar in both LEC and MEC.
source: In contrast, other intrinsic circuits from LVb to layers II and III (LII and LIII), which constitute hippocampal-entorhinal re-entry circuits, are very similar in both entorhinal subdivisions.
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The current view of the canonical hippocampal-cortical output circuit crucial for systems consolidation might need revision.
source: Our data seem to suggest that the current view of the canonical hippocampal-cortical output circuit that allegedly is crucial for systems consolidation might need revision, though the functional impact of our findings awaits further in vivo studies.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, explicitly noted as requiring further in vivo studies.

claim: In the MEC-13-53D transgenic mouse line, mCherry-positive neurons were observed mainly in LVb (93.2% in LEC and 82.9% in MEC).
source: In both LEC and MEC, mCherry-positive neurons were observed mainly in LVb (93.2% in LEC and 82.9% in MEC) and some in layer VI (LVI; 5.1% in LEC and 16.8% in MEC) but hardly in LVa (1.7% in LEC and 0.3% in MEC), and none in superficial layers (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the characterization of the transgenic mouse line, with data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the MEC-13-53D transgenic mouse line, some mCherry-positive neurons were observed in layer VI (5.1% in LEC and 16.8% in MEC).
source: In both LEC and MEC, mCherry-positive neurons were observed mainly in LVb (93.2% in LEC and 82.9% in MEC) and some in layer VI (LVI; 5.1% in LEC and 16.8% in MEC) but hardly in LVa (1.7% in LEC and 0.3% in MEC), and none in superficial layers (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the characterization of the transgenic mouse line, with data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the MEC-13-53D transgenic mouse line, mCherry-positive neurons were hardly observed in LVa (1.7% in LEC and 0.3% in MEC).
source: In both LEC and MEC, mCherry-positive neurons were observed mainly in LVb (93.2% in LEC and 82.9% in MEC) and some in layer VI (LVI; 5.1% in LEC and 16.8% in MEC) but hardly in LVa (1.7% in LEC and 0.3% in MEC), and none in superficial layers (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the characterization of the transgenic mouse line, with data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the MEC-13-53D transgenic mouse line, no mCherry-positive neurons were observed in superficial layers.
source: In both LEC and MEC, mCherry-positive neurons were observed mainly in LVb (93.2% in LEC and 82.9% in MEC) and some in layer VI (LVI; 5.1% in LEC and 16.8% in MEC) but hardly in LVa (1.7% in LEC and 0.3% in MEC), and none in superficial layers (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the characterization of the transgenic mouse line, with data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The proportion of PCP4-positive LVb neurons that show tTA-driven labeling was 45.9% in LEC and 30.9% in MEC.
source: The proportion of PCP4-positive LVb neurons that show tTA-driven labeling was 45.9% in LEC and 30.9% in MEC (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the characterization of the transgenic mouse line, with data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The percentage of tTA-expressing neurons that were PCP4-positive was 91.7% in LEC and 99.3% in MEC.
source: The tTA-driven labeling colocalized well with the PCP4 labeling (percentage of tTA-expressing neurons that were PCP4-positive was 91.7% in LEC and 99.3% in MEC; Figure 1F), highlighting the specificity of the line.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation demonstrating the specificity of the transgenic line, with data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The percentage of double-labeled (PCP4+, GAD67+) neurons among total GAD67-positive neurons is very low in both LEC and MEC (4.3% and 2.3%, respectively).
source: In another experiment using a GAD67 TG line expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP), we showed that the percentage of double-labeled (PCP4+, GAD67+) neurons among total GAD67-positive neurons is very low in both LEC and MEC (4.3% and 2.3%, respectively, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from an experiment using a GAD67 transgenic line, with data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The percentage of double-labeled (PCP4+, GAD67+) neurons was significantly lower than in the Ctip2-stained sample in both LEC (18.1%) and MEC (7.2%).
source: This percentage of double-labeled neurons was significantly lower than in the Ctip2-stained sample in both regions (18.1% for LEC and 7.2% for MEC).
evidence: This is a comparative quantitative observation with statistical significance implied.

claim: PCP4 can be used as a marker for excitatory entorhinal LVb neurons.
source: This result shows that PCP4 can be used as a marker for excitatory entorhinal LVb neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing low colocalization of PCP4 with GAD67.

claim: The MEC-13-53D is an attractive transgenic mouse line to target excitatory LVb neurons in both LEC and MEC.
source: The MEC-13-53D is thus an attractive TG mouse line to target excitatory LVb neurons in both LEC and MEC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the characterization data of the transgenic line.

claim: The apical dendrites of MEC-LVb neurons extend all the way up into layer I.
source: Neurons in MEC-LVb have an apical dendrite that heads straight to the pia, such that distal branches reach all the way up into LI, which is in line with previous studies (Canto and Witter, 2012a; Hamam et al., 2000; Sürmeli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a morphological observation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The apical dendrites of LEC-LVb neurons do not extend beyond layer III.
source: In contrast, the apical dendrites of LEC-LVb neurons have a more complex branching pattern and they do not extend beyond LIII.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the study.

claim: LEC-LVb neurons are unlikely to be targeted by inputs to LEC that selectively distribute to layers I and II, such as those carrying olfactory information from the olfactory bulb and the piriform cortex.
source: This indicates that LEC-LVb neurons are unlikely to be targeted by inputs to LEC that selectively distribute to layers I and II, such as those carrying olfactory information from the olfactory bulb and the piriform cortex (Luskin and Price, 1983) as well as commissural projections (Leitner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphological observation that LEC-LVb dendrites do not extend to layers I and II, combined with knowledge of input distributions.

claim: MEC-LVb neurons show a shorter time constant than LEC-LVb neurons.
source: The here reported differences between LVb neurons, with MEC-LVb neurons showing a shorter time constant than LEC-LVb neurons, further indicate that MEC-LVb neurons have a shorter time window to integrate inputs compared to LEC-LVb neurons (Canto and Witter, 2012a; Canto and Witter, 2012b).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological characterization of the neurons.

claim: MEC-LVb neurons have a shorter time window to integrate inputs compared to LEC-LVb neurons.
source: The here reported differences between LVb neurons, with MEC-LVb neurons showing a shorter time constant than LEC-LVb neurons, further indicate that MEC-LVb neurons have a shorter time window to integrate inputs compared to LEC-LVb neurons (Canto and Witter, 2012a; Canto and Witter, 2012b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the time constant data, supported by citations.

claim: Projections from principal neurons in LVb in both entorhinal subdivisions preferentially target pyramidal neurons in LIII and LII.
source: Both our anatomical and electrophysiological data show that projections from principal neurons in LVb in both entorhinal subdivisions preferentially target pyramidal neurons in LIII and LII.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study based on anatomical and electrophysiological data.

claim: LVb neurons have a weaker relationship with the class of stellate and fan cells in MEC or LEC, respectively.
source: LVb neurons have a weaker relationship with the class of stellate and fan cells in MEC or LEC, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: In both LEC and MEC, hippocampal information preferentially interacts with neurons that are part of the LIII-to-CA1/Sub projection system rather than with the LII-to-DG/CA2-3 projecting neurons.
source: This makes it likely that in both LEC and MEC hippocampal information preferentially interacts with neurons that are part of the LIII-to-CA1/Sub projection system rather than with the LII-to-DG/CA2-3 projecting neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectivity patterns observed.

claim: All LIII neurons (30 out of 30 cells) responded to optical stimulation of LVb fibers in MEC.
source: In line with this anatomical observation, all LIII neurons (30 out of 30 cells) responded to the optical stimulation (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the optogenetic experiments, with data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The percentage of pyramidal neurons in LII responding to optical stimulation of LVb fibers in MEC was 61.1% (11 out of 18 cells).
source: The percentage of pyramidal neurons in LII responding to optical stimulation was 61.1% (11 out of 18 cells), and this percentage was especially low in stellate cells (25.0%; 5 out of 20 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The percentage of stellate cells in LII responding to optical stimulation of LVb fibers in MEC was 25.0% (5 out of 20 cells).
source: The percentage of pyramidal neurons in LII responding to optical stimulation was 61.1% (11 out of 18 cells), and this percentage was especially low in stellate cells (25.0%; 5 out of 20 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Only 27.8% (5 out of 18 cells) of MEC-LVa neurons responded to optical stimulation of LVb fibers.
source: In line with this anatomical observation, only 27.8% (5 out of 18 cells) responded to the light stimulation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the optogenetic experiments, with data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The normalized voltage responses of LEC-LVa neurons were significantly larger than those of MEC-LVa neurons (0.93 ± 0.10 vs. 0.47 ± 0.10, p<0.05).
source: In contrast to the similar responses of LII neurons between the two subregions, the normalized voltage responses of LEC-LVa neurons were significantly larger than those of MEC-LVa neurons (0.93 ± 0.10 vs. 0.47 ± 0.10, p<0.05, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical analysis, with data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The response probabilities of LIIb, III, and Va neurons in LEC were high: 76.9% (20 out of 26 cells), 100% (34 out of 34 cells), and 94.7% (18 out of 19 cells), respectively.
source: On the other hand, the response probabilities of LIIb, III, and Va were high, 76.9% (20 out of 26 cells), 100% (34 out of 34 cells), and 94.7% (18 out of 19 cells), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the optogenetic experiments in LEC.

claim: Only 26.9% of the fan cells (7 out of 26 neurons) in LEC-LIIa responded to optical stimulation of LVb fibers.
source: In line with these anatomical observations, only 26.9% of the fan cells (7 out of 26 neurons) responded to the light stimulation (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the optogenetic experiments, with data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The normalized EPSP of LEC-LVa neurons based on LIII response was 0.93 ± 0.10.
source: the normalized voltage responses of LEC-LVa neurons were significantly larger than those of MEC-LVa neurons (0.93 ± 0.10 vs. 0.47 ± 0.10, p<0.05, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The normalized EPSP of MEC-LVa neurons based on LIII response was 0.47 ± 0.10.
source: the normalized voltage responses of LEC-LVa neurons were significantly larger than those of MEC-LVa neurons (0.93 ± 0.10 vs. 0.47 ± 0.10, p<0.05, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The weak experimental support for a strong LVb-to-LVa projection in dorsal MEC is not due to technical issues.
source: These data indicate that the weak experimental support for a strong LVb-to-LVa projection in dorsal MEC is not due to technical issues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the consistency of findings across different experimental approaches.

claim: The intrinsic LV circuitry that supposedly underlies the canonical hippocampal-cortical output circuit in dorsal MEC is differently organized than in other parts of EC.
source: Rather, the data provide evidence that the intrinsic LV circuitry that supposedly underlies the canonical hippocampal-cortical output circuit in dorsal MEC is differently organized than in other parts of EC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative data between MEC and LEC.

claim: The difference in connectivity from LVb to LVa between dorsal MEC and dorsal LEC has been recently corroborated in an in vitro study using paired-patch recording.
source: This difference in dorsal MEC, though unexpected in view of previous data including our own rabies tracing data (Ohara et al., 2018), has been recently corroborated in an in vitro study using paired-patch recording (Rozov et al., 2020), and our present corroborating tracing data are in line with previous tracing data in the rat (Köhler, 1986) and monkey (Chrobak and Amaral, 2007).
evidence: This statement references corroborating evidence from other studies.

claim: LVa neurons in MEC and LEC are rather similar in morphological and electrophysiological characteristics.
source: In contrast, LVa neurons in MEC and LEC are rather similar in these two aspects.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the characterization of neurons.

claim: LVb pyramidal neurons in LEC and MEC differ with respect to main morphological and electrophysiological characteristics.
source: First, the present data indicate that LVb pyramidal neurons in LEC and MEC differ with respect to main morphological and electrophysiological characteristics.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the morphological and electrophysiological characterization.

claim: In LEC, LVa neurons receive substantial input from LVb neurons.
source: Whereas in LEC, LVa neurons receive substantial input from LVb neurons, this projection is relatively weak in dorsal MEC.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The projection from LVb to LVa is relatively weak in dorsal MEC.
source: Whereas in LEC, LVa neurons receive substantial input from LVb neurons, this projection is relatively weak in dorsal MEC.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The sag ratio and AP frequency after 200 pA injection were smaller in LVa than LVb neurons.
source: Sag ratio (Figure 2C, F), time constant (Figure 2G), and AP frequency after 200 pA injection (Figure 2E, H) were the three prominent parameters that separated LVa and LVb neurons (Figure 2M) with the sag ratio and AP frequency after 200 pA injection being smaller in LVa than LVb, and the opposite was true for the time constant.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological characterization, with data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The time constant was larger in LVa than LVb neurons.
source: Sag ratio (Figure 2C, F), time constant (Figure 2G), and AP frequency after 200 pA injection (Figure 2E, H) were the three prominent parameters that separated LVa and LVb neurons (Figure 2M) with the sag ratio and AP frequency after 200 pA injection being smaller in LVa than LVb, and the opposite was true for the time constant.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological characterization, with data shown in Figure 2.

claim: MEC-LVb neurons showed a smaller time constant, higher AP frequency, and smaller fast AHP than LEC-LVb neurons.
source: Neurons in MEC-LVb showed a smaller time constant, higher AP frequency, and smaller fast AHP than LEC-LVb neurons.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the electrophysiological characterization.

claim: Many labeled axons of LEC-LVb neurons were present in LVa.
source: Although in both LEC and MEC, labeled axons were densely present in LIII rather than in layers II and I, we report a striking difference between LEC and MEC in LVa, as is easily appreciated from Figure 3L, M: many labeled axons of LEC-LVb neurons were present in LVa, whereas in case of MEC-LVb, the number of labeled axons was very low in LVa.
evidence: This is an anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments, with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In case of MEC-LVb, the number of labeled axons was very low in LVa.
source: Although in both LEC and MEC, labeled axons were densely present in LIII rather than in layers II and I, we report a striking difference between LEC and MEC in LVa, as is easily appreciated from Figure 3L, M: many labeled axons of LEC-LVb neurons were present in LVa, whereas in case of MEC-LVb, the number of labeled axons was very low in LVa.
evidence: This is an anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments, with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The normalized labeling was significantly higher in LEC-LVa than in MEC-LVa (p=0.0003).
source: The normalized labeling was significantly higher in LEC-LVa than in MEC-LVa (two-tailed paired t-test for LEC-LVa vs. MEC-LVa: t6 = 7.68, ***p=0.0003, LEC-LII vs. MEC-LII: t6 = 0.24, p=0.82).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical analysis, with data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: The normalized labeling in LII was not significantly different between LEC and MEC (p=0.82).
source: The normalized labeling was significantly higher in LEC-LVa than in MEC-LVa (two-tailed paired t-test for LEC-LVa vs. MEC-LVa: t6 = 7.68, ***p=0.0003, LEC-LII vs. MEC-LII: t6 = 0.24, p=0.82).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical analysis, with data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: The voltage responses of the more ventrally positioned LVa neurons in MEC were significantly higher than those measured more dorsally (p<0.01).
source: The voltage responses of the more ventrally positioned LVa neurons were significantly higher than those measured more dorsally in MEC (p<0.01, one-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni's multiple comparison test).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation with statistical analysis, examining dorsoventral differences in MEC, with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The EPSP amplitudes of LIII neurons did not differ at different dorsoventral levels in MEC.
source: Since the EPSP amplitudes of LIII neurons did not differ at different dorsoventral levels, it is unlikely that the observed response differences are caused by different levels of oChIEF expression in LVb fibers along the dorsoventral axis.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation used to rule out a technical explanation, with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: LVa cells in the dorsal MEC, irrespective of whether they have full or severed dendrites, did not respond to light stimulation.
source: This, however, does not seem to be the case since LVa cells in the dorsal MEC, irrespective of whether they have full (n = 3) or severed dendrites (n = 2), did not respond to light stimulation.
evidence: This is an observation ruling out severing of dendrites as an explanation for lack of responses, with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the ventral MEC recordings, four out of five neurons with seemingly intact dendrites responded to the optical stimulation.
source: In the ventral MEC recordings, four out of five neurons with seemingly intact dendrites responded to the optical stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from ventral MEC recordings, with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The latency of the EPSP onset for LII stellate cells was significantly longer than that for LIII cells (4.3 ± 0.7 vs. 2.9 ± 0.1 ms; p<0.5).
source: Note that the latency of the EPSP onset for LII stellate cells was significantly longer than that for LIII cells (4.3 ± 0.7 vs. 2.9 ± 0.1 ms; p<0.5, one-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni's multiple comparison test; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical analysis, with data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The inputs to LII pyramidal cells showed latencies similar to those of LIII cells (3.2 ± 0.2 vs. 2.9 ± 0.1 ms).
source: In contrast, the inputs to LII pyramidal cells showed latencies similar to those of LIII cells (3.2 ± 0.2 vs. 2.9 ± 0.1 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of latencies.

claim: The latency of the EPSP onset for LVa cells was significantly longer than that for LIII cells (5.6 ± 1.7 vs. 2.9 ± 0.1 ms; p<0.001).
source: In addition, the latency of the EPSP onset for LVa cells was significantly longer than that for LIII cells (5.6 ± 1.7 vs. 2.9 ± 0.1 ms; p<0.001, one-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni's multiple comparison test; Figure 4H), indicating that these responses are either the result of monosynatic inputs onto the apical dendrite in LIII or that they represent disynaptic responses.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical analysis and interpretation, with data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The latency of the EPSP onset in LEC was similar in all cell types (LIIa neurons, 4.8 ± 1.1; LIIb neurons, 5.0 ± 1.4; LIII neurons, 4.2 ± 0.9; LVa neurons, 4.2 ± 0.6 ms).
source: In line with our previous monosynaptic input tracing study using rabies virus (Ohara et al., 2018), the latency of the EPSP onset, which was similar in all cell types (LIIa neurons, 4.8 ± 1.1; LIIb neurons, 5.0 ± 1.4; LIII neurons, 4.2 ± 0.9; LVa neurons, 4.2 ± 0.6 ms; Figure 5H), points to the LVb-to-LVa connectivity, as well as that to LIII and LII, being largely monosynaptic.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation with interpretation, with data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The LVb-to-LVa connectivity in LEC, as well as that to LIII and LII, is largely monosynaptic.
source: In line with our previous monosynaptic input tracing study using rabies virus (Ohara et al., 2018), the latency of the EPSP onset, which was similar in all cell types (LIIa neurons, 4.8 ± 1.1; LIIb neurons, 5.0 ± 1.4; LIII neurons, 4.2 ± 0.9; LVa neurons, 4.2 ± 0.6 ms; Figure 5H), points to the LVb-to-LVa connectivity, as well as that to LIII and LII, being largely monosynaptic.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on latency data and previous rabies tracing studies.

claim: The input resistance of LIIa fan cells was significantly higher than that of LIIb and LIII neurons (LIIa neurons, 323.6 ± 16.1; LIIb neurons, 226.5 ± 17.2; LIII neurons, 194.3 ± 13.3 MΩ; p<0.001).
source: In contrast to MEC-LII stellate cells, the input resistance of LIIa fan cells was significantly higher than that of LIIb and LIII neurons (LIIa neurons, 323.6 ± 16.1; LIIb neurons, 226.5 ± 17.2; LIII neurons, 194.3 ± 13.3 MΩ; p<0.001, one-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni's multiple comparison test; Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical analysis, with data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The small responses of LIIa fan cells cannot be explained by the differences in input resistance among the superficial neurons.
source: This indicates that the small responses of LIIa fan cells cannot be explained by the differences in input resistance among the superficial neurons and may simply be due to the small number of synaptic inputs to LIIa fan cells from LVb neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the input resistance data.

claim: The small responses of LIIa fan cells may be due to the small number of synaptic inputs to LIIa fan cells from LVb neurons.
source: This indicates that the small responses of LIIa fan cells cannot be explained by the differences in input resistance among the superficial neurons and may simply be due to the small number of synaptic inputs to LIIa fan cells from LVb neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed small responses.

claim: LEC might be more relevant than MEC in mediating the export of information from the dorsal hippocampus to the neocortex.
source: It is clear that our current suggestion that LEC might be more relevant than MEC in mediating the export of information from the dorsal hippocampus to the neocortex needs to be substantiated in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the findings, explicitly noted as requiring in vivo substantiation.

claim: Both the stellate and the CB+ population of layer II pyramidal neurons contain grid cells.
source: First, both the stellate and the CB+ population of layer II pyramidal neurons contain grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005; Tang et al., 2014) and hippocampal excitatory inputs are required for the formation and translocation of grid patterns (Bonnevie et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on grid cells.

claim: Hippocampal excitatory inputs are required for the formation and translocation of grid patterns.
source: First, both the stellate and the CB+ population of layer II pyramidal neurons contain grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005; Tang et al., 2014) and hippocampal excitatory inputs are required for the formation and translocation of grid patterns (Bonnevie et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bonnevie et al., 2013.

claim: The two populations of grid cells (stellate vs. CB+ cells) might differ with respect to the strength of a main excitatory drive from the hippocampus.
source: Though our data do not exclude that LVb inputs can reach LII stellate cells indirectly through LIII- and LII-pyramidal cells (Ohara et al., 2019; Winterer et al., 2017), they do indicate that the two populations of grid cells, stellate vs. CB+ cells, might differ with respect to the strength of a main excitatory drive from the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: Re-entry of hippocampal activity has been proposed as one of the mechanisms for temporal storage of information in a neuronal network.
source: Second, re-entry of hippocampal activity, i.e., the presence of recurrent circuits, has been proposed as one of the mechanisms for temporal storage of information in a neuronal network (Edelman, 1989; Iijima et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Edelman, 1989 and Iijima et al., 1996.

claim: The circuit via LIII-CA1/subiculum in both entorhinal subdivisions is favored to mediate a recurrent hippocampal-entorhinal-hippocampal circuit.
source: Our current data strongly favor the circuit via LIII-CA1/subiculum in both entorhinal subdivisions to mediate a recurrent hippocampal-entorhinal-hippocampal circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the connectivity data.

claim: Entorhinal LIII input to the hippocampus field CA1 plays a crucial role in associating temporally discontinuous events and retrieving remote memories.
source: The importance of this layer III recurrent network is corroborated by the observation that entorhinal LIII input to the hippocampus field CA1 plays a crucial role in associating temporally discontinuous events and retrieving remote memories (Lux et al., 2016; Suh et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lux et al., 2016 and Suh et al., 2011.

claim: There is a direct projection from the intermediate/ventral hippocampus to neurons in MEC LVa.
source: Adding to this complexity is a recent report that there is a direct projection from the intermediate/ventral hippocampus to neurons in MEC LVa (Rozov et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rozov et al., 2020.
